title: October sales review: counting check
subtitle: Whether the October review can go to the leadership team on Friday, recounted from its queries and the sample data.

verdict.text: Do not send it as it is: the report says October is up 14.5%, but with all of September counted October is down 11.1%, EUR 85,390.00 against EUR 96,000.00.

sections.title: Findings
sections.intro: Every finding was read in the code and counted on the sample data.

items.title: September covers only 24 days, so a decline is reported as growth
items.evidence: Report: October up 14.5%, EUR 85,390.00 against EUR 74,607.00. The query stops September on the 24th and compares those 24 days with all 31 days of October. Full September on the sample: **EUR 96,000.00** (854 completed orders). Corrected change: **down 11.1%** (EUR 10,610.00 lower). Like for like it is worse: per day EUR 3,200.00 against EUR 2,754.52 (down 13.9%), and over the first 24 days EUR 74,607.00 against EUR 62,799.98 (down 15.8%).
items.fix: Change line 5 to `'2026-09-30'`. The headline becomes: October is down 11.1% on September, EUR 85,390.00 against EUR 96,000.00. By line, the fall is in premium (EUR 40,000.00 to EUR 26,000.00), while standard and value rose.

items.title: Conversion divides all orders by logged-in visits only
items.evidence: Report: 5.22% against a target of 4%. The top counts all 600 orders; the bottom counts only logged-in sessions, 11,500 of 23,000, although the query's comment says orders per visit. Corrected: 600 / 23,000 = **2.61%**. Logged-in orders over logged-in visits gives 299 / 11,500 = 2.60%, so the answer does not depend on which population was meant.
items.fix: Use `sum(sessions)` on lines 4 and 5. The headline becomes: web conversion was 2.61% in October, 1.39 points below the 4% target.

items.title: Desktop beats mobile only because mobile traffic is mostly paid social
items.evidence: Report: desktop 4.43%, mobile 1.81%, so move mobile budget to desktop. The two rates are counted correctly, but mobile leads inside every traffic source: direct 7.00% against 6.00%, search 3.50% against 3.00%, paid social 1.32% against 1.00%. Paid social is 87.5% of mobile sessions (14,000 of 16,000) and 14.3% of desktop sessions (1,000 of 7,000), and it converts near 1% on either device. At one common traffic mix, desktop is 2.35% and mobile 2.84% [high]. Each per-source gap is small for its counts, about one standard error, and a combined test gives z = 1.61 [med]. So the data does not prove mobile is better; it only removes the case for desktop.
items.fix: Group by `source, device`, and drop the budget proposal. The headline becomes: the gap between desktop and mobile comes from traffic mix; within each source mobile is level or slightly ahead.

items.title: The promotions join counts 40 orders twice
items.evidence: Report: net revenue EUR 88,600.00, while its own headline 3 gives October as EUR 85,390.00. The left join to `order_promotions` repeats the 40 orders that carry two promo codes, all on the standard line. Sum after the join EUR 88,600.00; correct sum **EUR 85,390.00** (the join adds EUR 3,210.00, or 3.8%). Standard becomes EUR 40,590.00 instead of EUR 43,800.00; premium and value do not change.
items.fix: Delete lines 6 and 7, since no column of `p` is used. The headline becomes: net revenue in October was EUR 85,390.00, led by the standard line at EUR 40,590.00.

items.title: The store average is a mean of six store means
items.evidence: Report: EUR 118.89. That is the plain mean of the six store averages, so store 6 with 6 orders weighs as much as store 1 with 120. The average over the 270 store orders is EUR 25,944.83 / 270 = **EUR 96.09**. The report is EUR 22.80, or 23.7%, too high.
items.fix: Replace it with one statement, `select sum(net_amount) / count(*)` under the same filters. The headline becomes: the average order in a store was EUR 96.09.

items.title: Store 6 is called the best store on 6 orders
items.evidence: Report: store 6 is the best store at EUR 240.00 and should be the model for the others. EUR 240.00 is correct, but it rests on **6 orders**, EUR 1,440.00 in total, the smallest revenue of the six stores. All six orders are premium, and premium store orders average EUR 205.53 across all stores [high], so the figure mostly reflects what was sold. Stores 5 (14 orders) and 4 (20 orders) are also under 30. Among stores with at least 30 orders the highest average is store 3, EUR 99.29 on 40 orders.
items.fix: Remove "best store" and the proposal. The headline becomes: store 6 is too small to rank, with 6 orders in October. Any ranking should use stores with at least 30 orders and compare within a product line.

items.title: The region filter also drops orders with no region
items.evidence: Report: the three regions brought EUR 81,842.62. `region <> 'unknown'` also drops NULLs: 30 completed October orders worth EUR 3,114.50, on top of 6 marked `unknown` worth EUR 432.88. The three named regions do add up to EUR 81,842.62, but with only `unknown` excluded the query totals **EUR 84,957.12**, and the report never says that EUR 3,547.38 (4.2%) of October's EUR 85,390.00 is outside them. No decision in the report rests on this number, so it is the least urgent of the high findings.
items.fix: Use `(region <> 'unknown' or region is null)` and label the extra row as no region. The headline becomes: north, south and west brought EUR 81,842.62; another EUR 3,547.38 (36 orders) has no usable region.

items.title: The chart exaggerates an increase that did not happen
items.evidence: The axis starts at EUR 70,000, so October's bar is drawn 3.3 times as tall as September's for values 1.14 times apart. September is the 24-day figure and the title says "Net revenue is growing". The full-month EUR 96,000.00 would run past the axis top of EUR 90,000. The values are typed into the notebook at line 20, not read from `output/sep_vs_oct.csv` as its heading says, so correcting the query will not correct the chart.
items.fix: Read the corrected CSV, remove `set_ylim` so the bars start at zero, and retitle it, for example "Net revenue fell 11.1% in October".

items.title: Not every saved output comes from the committed queries
items.evidence: The report says its numbers come from these queries and are saved under `output/`. EUR 118.89 is not in `output/`, and the second statement of `avg_order_by_store.sql` cannot run, because the `store_orders` CTE ends with the first statement at line 15 (it failed on the SQLite copy; CTEs have that scope in standard SQL [high]). `output/conversion.csv` has a `month` column the query does not select, and `output/avg_order_by_store.csv` is sorted by store while the query sorts by average. Every other saved number reproduces exactly.
items.fix: After the fixes, re-run every query and save its output directly, including the store average.

sections.title: What this review did not check

items: **The 4% target.** Nothing in the repository defines it, so I could not check whether it is set on all visits or on logged-in visits. Both readings give about 2.6%, below it.
**The effect of moving budget.** There is no spend or cost-per-visit data, so the review can only say the device comparison does not support the proposal.
**The production warehouse.** Only the sample was available. The queries ran on an in-memory SQLite copy of it, not on your warehouse.

**Whether October has changed since the refresh.** 32 October orders loaded more than 3 days after they were placed, up to 7.8 days, while no September order took more than 0.8 days [high]. All of them had loaded by 4 November, so they are in the data the report used. Anything that loaded after the sample was taken would move October.
**The drawn chart and the deck.** The notebook has no saved output, so I read its code and did not draw it. The Friday deck is not in the folder.
**Why revenue fell.** I counted it by product line only and did not analyse the causes.
**The finance ledger and the BI dashboard.** The report uses neither, so October was not reconciled to the ledger, and `reports/dashboards/` was not reviewed.

blocks.title: What I assumed
items: The sample is the data behind the report: every saved figure reproduced exactly on it, so corrected numbers are stated as the report's own population.

Net revenue means the finance definition in `models/marts/mart_net_revenue.sql`: completed orders, by order date, without shipping. The 8 staff orders (EUR 590.00) stay in, as they do in that definition.
September means the whole calendar month. Nothing in the report explains stopping at 24 September.
Conversion means orders per visit over all visits, as the comment on `conversion.sql:1` says.
The region filter was meant to drop only rows marked `unknown`, not rows with no region at all.
A store needs at least 30 orders to be ranked, the default of this review.
